He is incredibly apprehensive of strangers/loud noises/sudden movement and seems to be very selective about whom he will interact with. Upon reading his surrender note, I do not recommend a home with children or other animals. Likely requires a quiet/low energy home. He comes across as an old man with little patience for high activity. He was very friendly and loving when we were alone in the office.

She was able to leash/walk her & move her to a run with no issues. As soon as she got in the run & the door closed, she lunged while snarling. Seems very unpredictable. 10/27/2025 See intake behavior memo. Unpredictable. focus group: Liberty was barking and jumping at the gate  upon initial approach to her kennel. She stopped jumping and gently accepted treats through the gate with a tucked tail wag. Maddie walked around the door to make sure the outside part of her kennel was closed before we opened the guillotine. Liberty lunged at the gate and snarled at me when Maddie walked away. We opened the guillotine to let her over to the quieter side. She again accepted treats gently but did display some anxiety (tension around her eyes and mouth). I showed her the leash and she perked up. Easily leashed and retrieved. Pulled a bit on leash but manageable. She was aloof at first, completely ignoring Maddie and I in the yard unless Maddie offered her a treat. After a few minutes of her sniffing the yard, I stooped down on the ground and she came over to solicit attention. Liberty pushed her head into my hands and lap, rolling over for belly rubs. She then ran over to Maddie to solicit attention eagerly. When it was time to return her to the kennel, her anxiety returned (angled her body away from the kennel door, tense mouth and eyes, shifting her body weight back and forth). I walked into the kennel with her and pet her some more before slipping the leash off and closing the door. She rubbed her body against the door for pets again, no BR observed upon rekenneling. Leveling down from Staff Only to L3 BR. Behavior observed aligned with barrier reactivity. No concerning behaviors observed out of kennel.

Here is the meeting summary:Foster Consultation Summary — Farrell & ZazaDate: October 31st 2025Participants: Farrell (foster), Fina (trainer)Dog: Zaza — friendly, food-motivated, smart, working through dog-directed reactivity and excitable greetingsPrimary GoalsReduce reactivity to dogs/animals at a distance.Build calm, thinking responses in stimulating environments.Clean up polite greetings (reduce jumping).Establish low-stress routines and enrichment that support training.What’s Going WellSpiritDog work is helping with cars/people and general focus.Scatter feeding (“Go Sniff”), lick mats, KONGs, and snuffle mat are already in use.Loose-leash walking is improving; Zaza enjoys training and offers behaviors at home.Main Challenges Observed/DiscussedOff-leash neighborhood dog repeatedly derails walks; triggers reactivity and stress stacking.Reactivity specifically to distant dogs/animals.One growl during a lick-mat-in-crate scenario after an over-threshold walk (likely trigger stacking + guarding in safe space).Excited greeting/jumping at first contact.Management & Environment (next ~3 weeks)Avoid known triggers (walk in different locations/times; skip routes with the off-leash dog). Prevent rehearsals of reactivity.Keep overall stress low read more about trigger stacking and stress in dogs here: https://loyalpawrenting.pet/is-your-dogs-emotional-sink-overflowing/Walk quality over quantity: choose low-traffic times/places; consider fenced SniffSpots as enrichment: https://www.sniffspot.com/listings/woodstock-ga/my-favorite-farm-36789Daily Enrichment (target ~1/day)Continue licky mats, KONGs, scatter feeding. (Change the flavor often, try freezing as well)Increase chew-based options that are size appropriate (Himalayan chews, organic beef cheek rolls, trachea, coffee-wood sticks). Discontinue their use if, instead of chewing, he is just biting large chunks off and swallowing.Add calming music (Through a Dog’s Ear) at low volume. https://open.spotify.com/playlist/2BBxtIilmOtKVMe1pEJ0mH?si=73b37fefe920403eExploratory/sniff walks in new places when feasible.To learn what is enriching for your dog at different times, check out this blog post: https://loyalpawrenting.pet/dog-enrichment-isnt-optional-how-to-meet-your-dogs-most-overlooked-need/Training Plan (build thinking → outside)Marker Word/Clicker (load it): consistent “Yes!”/click → treat to clarify success.How dogs learn handout: https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fi/immki39mgfx3zdvqu2dhs/How-dogs-learn.pdf?rlkey=re27tesqg07xeijiqroi3c3td&st=lxeyusns&dl=0Clicker training 101 handout: https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fi/47tghwoh8vgxgyz87hqvu/Clicker-Training.pdf?rlkey=rypxuciu134xqjk0jv5n6wrbm&st=2aurw7rd&dl=0Touch/Hand Target (reorientation/recall): capture nose-to-palm at home; add cue when reliable; generalize gradually.Teach touch handout (follow phases): https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fi/nxwy33kdokemur5p7d2n4/Touch.pdf?rlkey=ql7lkdmf6bus388vt0odn86em&st=wike3pse&dl=0Auto Check-In (uncued attention): capture eye contact and pay in a slow 5–10-treat “conversation.” Start inside → add mild distractions → outside.Auto Check-In hanout: https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fi/bqwg58gkfdgb58gs6d0fr/Auto-Check-In.pdf?rlkey=99wdecbjr19yy5l9ypounsddt&st=p4kcc088&dl=0Class recommendation: https://suzanneclothier.com/shop/auto-check-in/Pattern Game “1-2-3” (management): load “Three,” then “Two–Three,” then “One–Two–Three.” Use to move past triggers without leash pulling.I don't have a handout, but here is a YouTube video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YEkYXk1skU0The only thing I don't like about this video is that the presenter does not let her dog sniff. Be careful to only practice this when Zaza has had a time to sniff around and is properly enriched. Keep it fun and short. This is just a management technique, so don't overdo it. If Zaza values sniffing more (because he hasn't had a chance to sniff enough) than the treat, then you will poison this cueReally Real Relaxation — helps dogs downshift and transition between arousal and calm. We ran out of time to discuss this in detail, but here is a Guardian training course:https://suzanneclothier.com/shop/really-real-relaxation-quick-course/Hanout: https://www.dropbox.com/scl/fi/27kdlnnrltvm0msayii72/Really-Real-Relaxation-Protocol.pdf?rlkey=wm2cm19apjaty5864k8cz6pt9&st=m1115dck&dl=0Generalization & Graduated Challenges: practice known cues outdoors in easy contexts; allow safe observation, then reinforce reorientation.Treats & Feeding NotesKibble is fine for easy reps; use higher-value (tiny, smelly, less 3 kcal) for outdoors/harder work (e.g., freeze-dried liver/heart/fish).Fig & Tyler Freeze dried treats 10% OFF Promo Code: PAWRENTBark Pouch treat pouches 10% OFF Promo Code: LOYALPAWRENT10 | You can find similar stuff on Amazon. Pull training portions from meals. Current 1 cup AM/PM seems more appropriate than prior higher amounts—please confirm with your vet for Zaza’s condition and food brand.Polite Greetings (reduce jumping)Pre-empt: if you see the “load-up,” mark (“Yes!”) and toss the treat to the floor before the jump.Reinforce four-on-the-floor with food/petting; withdraw attention the instant paws leave the ground; resume reinforcement when grounded.Crate & Resource Guarding PrecautionsCrate = safe space; avoid reaching in while he’s consuming food/lick mats.Prevent flips with secured lick mats.Teach Trade/Drop-It: We didn't have time to go too in-depth with this but here is my favorite video on how to teach a drop: https://youtu.be/ndTiVOCNY4M?si=tK3NKpnUeeQv1O4B

NoBest Way to Contact EmailFoster Dog Name (in shelter) JeremyGeneral Personality Jeremy (Bear is what he goes by) is generally a very chill and cuddly dog. He's happy to play all day with his sister or chew on a bone next to you, but his favorite activity in the world is fetch. He loves going for walks and car rides but he is still learning how to behave on a leash. I think he would be a good fit for anyone who wants a dog that's generally easy dog but still needs some training.Daily Routine Wake up around 830,go to the bathroom, play with my other dog until 10. Nap time (usually in a crate) 10-2ish, either a walk or more doggy play until 3 or 4. 4-6 is another crate nap. 6-8 training or a walk and more free time. 8 is dinner and then settle down for the nightWhat food do they eat? Purina oneWhat would be an ideal home and family for your foster? He's fairly adaptable. He can live with children and/ or another dog. Untested with cats. The main thing is that he needs someone who is calm under pressure or experienced with dogs. He's prone to feeling anxious/insecure and if his owner reacts with more anxiety, he can become unmanageable. So if we're walking and he sees another dog, he will lunge at it. If his handler responds by pulling back on the leash or hovering over him or yelling, it will make it worse. If his handler responds calmly, he'll calm down.On a scale of 1 to 5... how housetrained are they? 5Does your foster use a kennel without excessive barking/whining, escape attempts, or destruction? No exposureDo they prefer men or women? No preferenceDoes he / she live with another dog? YesHas he / she been around other dogs? He has been great with every dog I've intentionally introduced him to (they meet either through walking together or sniff through a crate before playing). He and my current dog play constantly, there is zero aggression or resource guarding of food, toys, territory, or people. HOWEVER he has a bite history with dogs that he has met at dog parks (this was through his previous adopter). I suspect this stemmed from insecurity rather than aggression, but any adopters should avoid dog parks.Does he / she know any basic commands? Which ones (Sit, stay, come, lay down, etc) ? He knows sit, stay, leave it, come, lay down, and go to your crate.Is your foster dog leash reactive? What makes them bark/lunge on leash? He is not great on a leash. But balls are definitely his favorite.Tell us a fun story about your foster... The relationship between Bear and my current dog is adorable. She is almost twice his size but half his age, and she is such an energetic little sister, but Bear is the best, most patient older brother a gal could ask for. She will often lie in his crate with him as he eats his food or chews a bone. If she tries to steal the bone, he will let her take it and then pretend to go for another toy (knowing that she'll follow) just to take the bone back. He just lies on his back and happily wags his tail as she tugs at his ears. It's very cute.I love my foster and think he/she is fabulous because _____________? He is such a great companion. In the morning, I can open the door and he immediately goes down the steps and through the gate to the back yard where he does his business and comes right back inside.What makes him/her nervous or unhappy? 3/4/2025 Google doc:https://docs.google.com/document/d/12VRZbec5PdplO1XKaDgVG3t8xgSpf__i1z994XBE-vg/edit?usp=sharingPrimary Presenting Issues:Separation AnxietyReactivity to other dogsReactivity to strange menBackground/History:Two year old, 56 lbs, spayed maleTrazodone 100mg 2 tablets, once ever 12 hrs. Theo has been with Nelly for two monthsAverage of 4-5 hrs home alone (without human companionship)Knows sit, lay down, stay, waitTheo seems to do better with strange males in his own house compared to other environments. Nelly described some interactions with other dogs but it’s hard for me to tell if Theo was being playful or aggressive without video of it. For the moment I have asked Nelly to stop dog-to-dog interactions until Theo has some more skills and feels more confident. I am referring Nelly to Malena DeMartini website for separation anxiety help with a licenced professional. Primary Care Veterinarian: LifeLine Animal Shelter Veterinarian Food/Feeding Schedule: Daily Fresh 3 cups a day, 7am, 1pm, 7pm.Medical Issues:No known medical issuesExercise:Out for potty 5 times a day10-15 min walk three times a day30 min walk 1-2 times a dayFetch and walking around the yard 2-3 times a dayTraining:No known formal training historyEquipment:Body harness6 ft leashRecommendations:It is incredibly important to manage Theo’s environment so that he does not get a chance to rehearse the undesirable behaviors. If you see that he has already spotted an other dog approaching, move the other way to gain some distance from the other dog. It’s important to not prompt Theo to perform a cue that he is not ready to perform or has not practice under those circumstances. Remember, practice makes perfect. Practice all the suggested behaviors in different situations and environments where Theo is successful. Slowly practice outdoors as Theo’s confidence increases and starts to offer unprompted check-ins. Practice scenarios that you have experienced in the past without the distraction. Work on distance, distraction and duration as three separate levels of difficulty. See below a list of activities you can do to help Theo with his reactivity and also to meet strangers.Confidence:Sniffing GamesFind it! This is a great game to play encouraging your dog to find a treat (or toy if he has a favorite toy). Show your dog a treat or his favorite toy, and then place it out of his sight but easily accessible. Tell him to “Find it!”. Once he finds it praise enthusiastically. You can start to increase the difficulty of the game by turning off the lights, adding more treats, using boxes or even hiding treats in less conventional places like inside of a shoe. The rewards for the dog are multiple- he gets a treat or finds his toy plus a very happy handler. If issuing a toy, be sure to reward his find with some play before starting again. When multiple treats or toys are used, this particular game helps to build persistence and trust in the handler. The dog may initially find only 2 out of 3 treats, but he quickly discovers that persistence in searching when you give the “Find it!” cue pays off. He learns to believe you - there really is another one there! FreeworkIntroduction to FreeworkPlace snuffle mats and licky mats around an rea of your hours and load them with treats, yogurt, peanut butter, etc… Let your dog go in and explore the area while enjoying the amazing treats you set out for him. Don’t give him big pieces, this activity is more about the journey of finding the treats. Try using small crumbs so encourage more sniffing. You can also use your dog’s kibble for this. This game allows your dog to freely go in an area and explore. You can also do the same set-up outdoors to encourage him to sniff in situations where he might want to bark otherwise. Scatter FeedScatter Feeding Dogs: A Step-by-Step Guide To Our Favourite Calm Enrichment Activity!Why scatter feeding is beneficial for dogsScatter feeding provides a way for Theo to use his nose and calm down. You can use the same cue as “Find it!”. Do this in your back yard or even Sniffspots! Consent TestPetting Consent Tests movieParticing this form of consent testing will help Theo have some predictability when meeting strangers. Knowing that he wont be petted unless requested can be very empowering for dogs. When Theo meets strangers, please encourage your visitors to not do strong eye contact or talk to Theo at least initially. Let Theo do some freework or scatter feet for some minutes while he is adjusting to the presence of the new visitor. Communication:Teach Unprompted Attention/Auto Check-InAuto Check-In.pdfI am attaching a handout on how to do this but here is a short course on how to teach it with some demo videos: https://suzanneclothier.com/shop/autocheckin/This is very similar to the “Look at me” cue with the difference that it’s coming from the inside out where the dog is voluntarily offering attention. Puppy Politeness PokerPractice Puppy Politeness Poker by creating a list of reliable cues Theo will enthusiastically perform. Also create a list of real-life rewards that he will work for (meal time, access to a snuffle mat, opening a door, etc). Utilize those cues to give him explicit permission to access something he wants and change it up every time. This will teach Theo to slow down, listen to your request and work for what he wants. Teaches impulse control, attention and it polishes the communication between you and him. You can learn more about this concept by watching this free webinar: https://suzanneclothier.com/member_video_library/puppy-politeness-poker-webinar/Training:Teaching TouchTouch.pdfOnce Theo is able to give a “Touch” when cued in different situations, you can start using this cue during walks when you see that he spots an other dog and want to prevent him from reacting. You might need to use smellier rewards in the beginning. Practice WaitI don’t have a hand-out for wait but it sounds like Theo already knows this behavior and he just need to practice. Start small with baby steps. Take one step at a time to build distance. Once you are able to ask Theo to wait and go to a different room you can start working on duration. Once Theo is able to wait for a longer period of time you can throw in distractions like maybe closing a door and then opening it. The more you practice this, the easier it will be for him once you take it outside and introduce it in the stairs. Remember to start out with baby steps, even through Theo already has mastered “Wait” with distance, duration and distractions in-doors, you still want to start with just one step outdoors. Management:Teach 1-2-3 Treat! https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ui6dWBDdDScI wasn’t able to find any great videos of this (I should make my own lol) but basically you condition your dog to expect a treat when they hear the word “three”. If you practice this in-doors with no distractions, you eventually will be abe to do this outdoors. When you see another dog coming then you can perform the pattern that Theo already knows and he will prefer to be next to you waiting for the treat instead of reacting to the other dog. Emergency “U” turnTeaching an Emergency U Turn Portland Dog Training/ Teach an Emergency U-Turn for your Reactive Dog/ Noble Woof Dog TrainingTeaching Theo an Emergency “U” turn will help you get out of situations where he is likely to react. By practicing this, you will be able to prevent him from practicing the undesirable behavior. Scatter FeedAfter Theo has had a lot of practice with the “Find it” cue, you can do a scatter feed during walks when you see there is a dog approaching on the opposite site of the street. Please be mindful that this would be done if you are sure that the other dog is not walking towards you or wont approach you. This is meant as a management technique to prevent him from reacting to an other dog and rehearse the undesirable behavior. TouchOnce Theo learns touch, you can also do this to basically step aside and call him over buy asking him to touch. This will allow you to position him an a way where he is not facing the other dog approaching and will buy you some time while the other dog finishes crossing. Follow up:I recommend booking an in-person appointment to work on counter conditioning and desensitizing Theo to other dogs during walks and address reactivity issues. Additionally we can work practicing polite greetings with strangers. To book your next in-person appointment please visit https://loyalpawrenting.pet/ → Book Now → First Let’s Meet → Step 2: In-Home Assessment.During this 1.5 hr visit, we will work on creating a customized training, enrichment and management plan to set up Theo for success. We will also perform a Relationship Assessment Test to determine behavior patterns in your relationship with Theo. If you are interested in self-paced training I recommend taking the following course by Victoria Stillwell: https://positively.com/learning/course/help-stop-reactivity

He would occasionally come up to the gate to see what I was doing but then immediately retracted to the back of the kennel. He would low growl with whale eyes if I turned around. Realizing that he was more scared then anything, I cracked the run door open to see if he would approach. As soon as the run door opened and I offered my hand for a sniff, he approached me with a low-wagging tail. I offered him my leash to which he lowered his head and allowed me to put it on. Exited the kennel and walked to the mulch yard. When we got into the mulch yard, I let him roam around (with the leash still on). I sat on the bench and allowed him to approach me if he wanted. I observed that he was heavily panting due to stress. However, he would approach me with a wagging tail and allow me to pet his head and back. We left the mulch yard and went for a walk to the next yard over where he did a fence greeting with Bubba Boy. He seemed excited to meet another dog and I suspect he is dog friendly. We then walked inside and I brought him over to the supervisor desk. He stopped midway to greet two customers in which he offered submissive ears and a tail wag. Once at the desk, he was met by a few kennel techs. While he did show some shyness, he allowed one kennel tech to pet his head. We went back to 200, I placed him back in his kennel and unleashed without incident. Recommend L3-SF and a playgroup assessment.

He would pause, briefly pin his ears back and then keep walking away. Generally aloof with us if we did not have food. I stood up and he sniffed around the yard a few more times, walked over to Maddie to solicit attention from her, before walking back over to me.
